issue.description:
## Problem

The /readyz fallback path (when canary is not running) calls HeadBucket via the AWS SDK, which maps to a Class C (paid) operation in B2's S3-compatible API.

## Solution

Remove the HeadBucket fallback entirely. Use the manifest writer's last successful delta flush timestamp as the health signal instead — this is already in memory from normal operation and costs zero B2 API calls.

## New readyz logic

- Canary running + healthy → 200 (zero B2 calls)
- Canary running + unhealthy → 503 (zero B2 calls)
- Manifest writer last flush within threshold → 200 (zero B2 calls)
- None of the above → 503

## Changes required

- Add LastFlush() time.Time accessor to manifest.Writer
- Update Server.readyz to check manifest writer flush time as fallback before HeadBucket
- Remove HeadBucket call from readyz (and backendHealthCache if no longer needed)
- Update readyz tests to cover manifest-writer fallback path
- Update TestReadyzConcurrentCachedHead to use manifest writer path instead of HeadBucket
issue.title: readyz: replace HeadBucket fallback with manifest last-flush health signal

issue.description:
## Summary
Build the restore-verification harness from plan.md Phase 6: a long-running verifier (Deployment with an internal scheduling loop -- per the no-CronJobs convention, not a Job/CronJob) that, per bucket, restores (a) the most recent backup object set and (b) a random sample of historical objects, through two independent paths:

1. The normal ARMOR read path (S3 GetObject through the running server)
2. armor-decrypt directly against raw B2 ciphertext with the escrowed MEK (bypassing ARMOR entirely -- proves the "ARMOR server is gone" recovery path works, not just that the server currently works)

Verify plaintext SHA-256 against manifest/provenance records on both paths, and that the two paths agree with each other.

## Why this matters now
bf-1v6skf / bf-24sxh7 (P0, found 2026-07-14/15) proved that a real backup can look completely healthy (object exists, right size, canary green) while being unrestorable. Nobody would have caught this without a human manually running litestream restore. This harness is what makes that kind of discovery automatic and continuous instead of accidental.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Deployment (not Job/CronJob) with an internal ticker/scheduling loop, one per configured bucket or shared across buckets with per-bucket state
- Restores most-recent generation + a random historical sample on each run
- Both paths implemented: ARMOR read path (real S3 client) and armor-decrypt direct-to-ciphertext
- Plaintext SHA-256 compared against manifest/provenance records; mismatch or restore failure is a hard failure, not a warning
- Runs against all in-scope buckets: armor-apexalgo, ord-devimprint, iad-ci, iad-kalshi, rs-manager

## Related
- bf-1v6skf, bf-24sxh7 (the concrete bug this would have caught)
- bf-2t1f (Phase 5 version-drift check -- this harness should be able to correlate failures against deployed version)
- Phase 6 genesis
issue.title: Phase 6: Build dual-path restore-verification harness

issue.description: Live verification 2026-07-19 of the bf-5tol4d implementation: a 50MB aws s3 cp with DEFAULT concurrency fails every time with InvalidPartSize - all 7 parts start concurrently, the short final part (least bytes) completes FIRST, P gets pinned to the final-part size and the first full-size part invalidates the upload. The implementation matched the original ADR spec; the spec rarity assumption was wrong - this is the COMMON case whenever part count fits the concurrency window (most files under ~80MB with aws cli defaults). Fix per the ADR-005 Amendment section (pushed): (1) pin P ONLY from part number 1; (2) a part arriving before part 1 has pinned P gets a retryable 503 SlowDown response with nothing stored - standard clients retry transparently; (3) keep the existing contradiction-poisoning as defense-in-depth for clients that never send part 1. ACCEPTANCE: 50MB aws-cli-DEFAULT-concurrency round-trip byte-identical (the exact failing repro); existing shuffled/sequential/retry tests stay green; a test where parts 2..N arrive before part 1 and succeed after SlowDown retries; go test -race green.
issue.title: ADR-005 P-pinning: pin from part 1 + SlowDown-defer earlier parts (default-concurrency uploads fail today)

issue.description: tests/integration/integration_test.go TestMultipartUpload does a real 3-part 15MB multipart upload/download cycle but only asserts ContentLength matches expected size -- never reads back and compares actual bytes. Change it to seed each part with distinguishable, verifiable content and compare full downloaded bytes against what was uploaded. Add sibling test cases: a final part that is not a multiple of part size, and a single-part multipart upload. Confirm this test actually gates the image-build/CI pipeline that produces deployed images -- a content-correctness regression should never be able to ship.
issue.notes:
[migrated notes from bf-28rb]
REOPENED 2026-07-15: verified the prior completion is inadequate. internal/backend/multipart_integration_test.go (TestMultipartUpload and its three siblings) do real-looking multipart upload/download cycles and do compare byte-for-byte content -- but ALL FOUR run against mockBackendForMultipart (same file, ~line 555), a pure in-memory Go map that concatenates part bytes directly. It never calls internal/crypto (no Encrypt, no Decrypt, no HMAC verification anywhere) and never talks to a real S3/B2 endpoint. It is structurally incapable of catching any encryption/decryption/HMAC bug, including bf-1v6skf (the P0 currently open: large multipart objects fail HMAC verification on real GetObject). The docstring claims this test "gates the CI pipeline" against content-correctness regressions -- it does not and cannot, regardless of CI wiring (bf-180ohh verified CI wiring, not test validity).

Corrected acceptance criteria:
- Test must exercise ARMOR's real request path: either the actual running armor server (S3 API surface) backed by a real or realistic backend, or at minimum internal/crypto's real Encrypt/Decrypt/HMAC-verify functions wired into the multipart assembly -- not a map-based mock
- Must reproduce at the scale where bf-1v6skf actually failed (44MB level-9-snapshot-equivalent object, not just the existing 15MB/3-part mock scenario) -- the current mock tests would still pass even if real, since they never got near the actual failing block boundary
- Must assert full decrypt success AND HMAC verification success on GetObject/range-read, not just that stored bytes match a map lookup
- Should be added as (or alongside) a true integration test that hits ARMOR over HTTP with real crypto enabled, so a future "looks real but mocks the crypto layer" regression is itself structurally impossible

Acceptance criteria: exercise the REAL internal/crypto encrypt/decrypt path end-to-end at >=44MB with multiple block-aligned parts and out-of-order completion, verifying downloaded bytes equal uploaded bytes per part. A mock-only test does NOT satisfy this bead. Must gate CI image builds.

issue.description:
WHY: ARMOR is the encryption layer for backup/archive pipelines (an archive-to-B2 pipeline for another project is blocked on ARMOR maturing). The 2026-03-27 data-loss incident motivated encryption. A backup is only durable if it can be recovered WITHOUT a running ARMOR server: today the only decryptor is the live proxy (cmd/armor/main.go is server-only, no subcommands; scripts/ has only verify-cloudflare-setup.sh). docs/plan/plan.md 'Decisions and Rationale' claims 'envelope enables offline reading' but no tool exists.

WHAT: a standalone decrypt tool, either a subcommand (e.g. 'armor decrypt') in cmd/armor or a separate cmd/armor-decrypt binary, that:
- reads an encrypted envelope from a local file OR fetches from B2/HTTPS URL
- parses the envelope header (magic ARMR, version byte, block size, IV, plaintext size, block count — see plan.md 'Encrypted Object Format'), falling back to x-amz-meta-armor-* metadata when needed
- unwraps the DEK using a MEK supplied via env var or flag (hex, 32 bytes); supports named multi-key MEKs via x-amz-meta-armor-key-id
- verifies per-block HMAC-SHA256 (HKDF-derived key, info=armor-hmac-v1) and reports integrity failures per block
- handles multipart-uploaded objects whose HMAC table lives in the .armor/hmac/<sha256-of-key> sidecar (envelope reserved-byte flag; see plan.md 'Multipart Upload Operations')
- writes verified plaintext to stdout or a file
Reuse internal/crypto (envelope.go, decryptor.go, keys.go, hkdf.go) — no new crypto.

ACCEPTANCE:
- go build produces the tool; unit test round-trips: encrypt via internal/crypto, decrypt via the tool code path (single-part and sidecar-HMAC cases)
- Decrypting a sample envelope with only the MEK (no B2 credentials, no server config) succeeds
- Wrong MEK and corrupted block produce clear, non-zero-exit errors
- README.md gains a 'Disaster recovery / offline decryption' section documenting usage
- No secrets, keys, or bucket names hardcoded
issue.title: Offline decrypt/recovery CLI — restore objects with only MEK + B2 ciphertext

issue.description:
Verify the multipart/HMAC decrypt fix with an INDEPENDENT large-object round-trip that does
not depend on the queue-api litestream chain, and that additionally exercises ranged reads.

## Why this bead exists

bf-1v6skf holds the multipart/HMAC decrypt bug. Its code fix is already confirmed live: a
real 56.6MB production object was GET+decrypted byte-exact through the fleet on 0.1.1901
(2026-07-22), spanning roughly 864 blocks -- well past the historical failure point. But
that bead cannot close, because its acceptance criterion is specifically a
queue-api/litestream restore transcript, and that chain has no compacted snapshot to test
against yet. As of 2026-07-26 the queue-api replica in B2 contains only small level-0
segments (about 4KB to 385KB), so a large-object restore cannot be demonstrated there for
some time.

This bead unblocks the confidence question without waiting on litestream. It is NOT a
replacement for the bf-1v6skf acceptance criterion -- that bead should still close on its
own transcript. This one provides independent evidence, on the cluster that matters, and
covers a path litestream never touches.

## Why Parquet specifically

A litestream restore is a sequential whole-object read. It never exercises ranged reads.
DuckDB reading Parquet over S3 does the opposite: it issues HTTP range requests for the
footer and then for selected row groups. ARMOR translates plaintext ranges to ciphertext
ranges over AES-256-CTR, so ranged decrypt is a genuinely distinct code path from whole-file
decrypt, and it is the exact access pattern the commitgraph aggregator uses. Testing with a
Parquet file covers both paths in one artifact and gives a known-good local baseline to
compare against.

## Sizing rationale (do not shrink this)

- ord-devimprint runs ARMOR_BLOCK_SIZE=65536, i.e. 64 KiB blocks.
- The historical failure was at block 256, which at 64 KiB is 16 MiB.
- A 100MB object is roughly 1600 blocks, about 6x past that point.
- The existing canary defaults to a 6MB multipart object, which is only about 96 blocks --
  BELOW block 256. The canary therefore cannot catch this class of bug at its default size.
  That gap is worth its own bead; note it rather than silently relying on the canary.
- B2 requires a 5 MiB minimum part size for non-final multipart parts, so a 100MB object
  yields a genuine multi-part upload rather than a single-part write.

## Preferred approach

Option A -- reuse an existing large object. If a corpus Parquet of at least ~100MB already
exists in a bucket fronted by the ord-devimprint ARMOR, verify against that first. Cheapest
and tests real production data. Requirement: it must have been WRITTEN by 0.1.1901 or later.
The bug was specifically that ARMOR could not decrypt objects it wrote itself, so verifying
against an object written by an older build proves nothing about the fix.

Option B -- generate a purpose-built Parquet of about 100MB. Preferred if no qualifying
object exists, and better for the ranged-read half of the test because it gives an exact
local baseline. Use multiple row groups (so row-group skipping actually issues distinct
ranges), a mix of column types, and enough rows that predicate pushdown selects a strict
subset.

## Test steps

1. Create or identify the object. Record its exact byte length and sha256 before upload.
2. PUT it through the ord-devimprint ARMOR service, not directly to the backend. It must be
   ARMOR that performs the encryption and multipart assembly.
3. Whole-object read: GET it back through ARMOR, confirm the returned length matches
   Content-Length exactly, and confirm sha256 matches the pre-upload value. A byte-count
   match alone is insufficient -- the historical corruption produced correctly-sized output.
4. Ranged read at the old failure boundary: request an explicit byte range that straddles
   block 256 (offset 16777216). Confirm those bytes match the same offsets in the local
   source file. This is the single most important assertion in this bead.
5. Ranged reads via DuckDB: point DuckDB at the object through ARMOR and run
   read_parquet over it. Confirm row count matches the local baseline, and run at least one
   aggregate (for example a SUM and a COUNT with a WHERE clause that forces row-group
   skipping) whose result matches running the same query against the local file.
6. Confirm from ARMOR logs that the DuckDB queries actually produced ranged requests rather
   than whole-object fetches -- otherwise step 5 silently degrades into a repeat of step 3.
7. Delete the test object afterwards if Option B was used.

## Routing and cost -- read before running

The ord-devimprint ARMOR sets ARMOR_CF_DOMAIN to a Cloudflare-fronted host, so downloads
through it egress via the Cloudflare edge, which is free under the Bandwidth Alliance.
Uploads to Backblaze are free ingress.

Do NOT run this test against the raw Backblaze S3 endpoint. That bypasses Cloudflare and
turns a free test into billable B2 egress. The intended data path is up through the
Backblaze endpoint and back down through the Cloudflare edge network. If the test is run
from inside the cluster, confirm the client resolves the ARMOR service and that ARMOR is
using its CF domain for the download leg.

## Acceptance criteria

- sha256 of the full round-tripped object matches the source exactly.
- A ranged read straddling offset 16777216 returns bytes identical to the local source at
  those offsets.
- DuckDB read_parquet through ARMOR returns a row count and at least one aggregate identical
  to the same query run against the local file.
- Evidence that ranged requests were actually issued (ARMOR log lines or Content-Range
  responses), not just whole-object GETs.
- A pasted transcript of the commands and their output. Do not close on a prose assertion
  that it worked -- bf-1v6skf was falsely closed four times between 07-15 and 07-18, each
  time reopened on live re-verification. Paste the evidence.
- The ARMOR build under test is recorded explicitly (expected: 0.1.1901 or later on
  ord-devimprint).

## Notes

- Test on ord-devimprint. That is the cluster commitgraph runs on, and the one whose
  large-object DR is still unproven. The 07-22 verification was on iad-kalshi.
- An operator kubeconfig with write access to ord-devimprint was obtained 2026-07-26, which
  was the gating dependency recorded in bf-2p1wr.

issue.description:
cmd/armor-decrypt builds an S3 client from ARMOR_B2_ENDPOINT and has no Cloudflare branch at all. The ARMOR service reads via ARMOR_CF_DOMAIN and falls back to direct S3 only when it is empty (internal/backend/b2.go GetRangeWithHeaders), so the service gets free Bandwidth Alliance egress while the break-glass tool always spends billed B2 egress.

Measured 2026-08-08 on one 154MB object: Cloudflare ~7.9 MB/s (free), direct B2 S3 ~38 MB/s (billed).

Not a correctness issue and arguably the right trade in a real emergency (a multi-GB restore costs cents, and speed matters more), but it should be a deliberate choice rather than a silent one. Now documented in docs/disaster-recovery.md.

The two are NOT interchangeable: ARMOR_CF_DOMAIN fronts B2's native download API (/file/<bucket>/<key>) with a different auth scheme, not the S3 API — so this needs a real code path, not a config flag.

Worth doing if offline restores become routine rather than exceptional.
issue.title: armor-decrypt cannot use the Cloudflare path — offline restore always bills egress

issue.description:
## Bug

ARMOR pod on ord-devimprint (namespace: devimprint) is in CrashLoopBackOff with 67+ restarts over 19h.

**Symptoms:**
- ARMOR starts fine, logs show successful startup listening on :9000
- After ~90s, receives SIGTERM and exits cleanly (exit code 0)
- Cycle repeats

**Known facts:**
- `/healthz` (liveness probe) always returns 200 — pure liveness, no backend checks
- `/readyz` (readiness probe) uses in-memory canary status, returns 503 if unhealthy
- Readiness probe failures do NOT kill pods — only liveness failures do
- Exit code 0 rules out OOM (would be 137)
- ARMOR handles SIGTERM gracefully with 3-phase shutdown (60s timeout per phase)
- Liveness config: http://:9000/healthz, initialDelay=10s, period=30s, failureThreshold=3
  → would kill after 10 + 3×30 = 100s (matches observed ~90s)

**What to investigate:**
1. Check ARMOR container logs for panics or fatal errors before the SIGTERM — a goroutine panic
   could kill the HTTP server, making /healthz unreachable, triggering liveness failure
2. Check if B2 backend is reachable from the ORD cluster — if ARMOR can't connect to B2 at all,
   it may panic during the first canary round-trip
3. Check ARMOR stderr for Go runtime panics (may not appear in stdout logs)
4. Verify the armor image version matches the source — the deployment comment says v0.1.5 but
   the actual image tag may differ
5. Check ARMOR startup env vars — missing B2 credentials could cause immediate failure

**Kubeconfig note:**
The ord-devimprint kubeconfig token expired 2026-04-26 19:10 EDT. Must be refreshed before
investigating. The cluster is a Rackspace Spot cluster — re-login via Spot dashboard to get
a new token.

## Deployment
- Manifest: `k8s/ord-devimprint/devimprint/armor-deployment.yml` in declarative-config
- Image: `ronaldraygun/armor:latest` (should be pinned)
- Resources: 50m CPU / 128Mi req, 512Mi limit

## Impact
Website-builder cannot connect to armor:9000 for S3 data. No new site builds are being
produced. The DevImprint leaderboard CSS fix is deployed but can't take effect until armor
recovers and website-builder completes a build cycle.
issue.title: armor: CrashLoopBackOff on ord-devimprint — SIGTERM after ~90s uptime

issue.description:
## Child Bead: Verify decoded value is human-readable and not corrupted

This bead performs final validation that the decoded value is clean, readable text with no corruption.

### Prerequisites
- Previous child bead complete (bf-1y0g6: value matches AWS access key format)

### Acceptance Criteria
- Value contains only printable ASCII characters
- No control characters, null bytes, or binary data
- No trailing/leading whitespace (except newline)
- Value is not garbled or corrupted
- Hex dump shows clean ASCII

### Commands
```bash
# Display the value one more time for confirmation
echo "Final decoded value:"
cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
echo ""

# Check for non-printable characters (should be none)
if cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | grep -P '[[:cntrl:]]' > /dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: File contains control characters"
    cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | od -c | head -5
    exit 1
else
    echo "No control characters detected"
fi

# Check for null bytes
if cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | grep -P '\x00' > /dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: File contains null bytes"
    exit 1
else
    echo "No null bytes detected"
fi

# Show hex dump to verify clean ASCII
echo "Hex dump (first 40 bytes):"
xxd -l 40 /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt

# Verify file type
FILETYPE=$(file -b /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt)
echo "File type: $FILETYPE"

if echo "$FILETYPE" | grep -qiE 'text|ascii'; then
    echo "SUCCESS: File is clean text/ASCII data"
else
    echo "WARNING: Unexpected file type"
fi

# Final confirmation
VALUE=$(cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | tr -d '[:space:]')
echo ""
echo "=== VALIDATION COMPLETE ==="
echo "Decoded AWS Access Key ID: $VALUE"
echo "Length: ${#VALUE} characters"
echo "File: /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt"
```

Success: Value is clean, human-readable ASCII with no corruption.

Failure: Value contains control chars, null bytes, or binary corruption — secret may be corrupted.
issue.title: Verify decoded value is human-readable and not corrupted

issue.description:
## Context

`queue-db` and `forgejo-postgres` (CNPG PostgreSQL, both on `iad-ci`) are the
only two barman-cloud backup targets in the estate that write through ARMOR
(`endpointURL: http://armor.armor.svc.cluster.local:9000`). `queue-db` has
failed **every** scheduled base backup since 2026-05-26 (600+ consecutive
`InvalidPartSize` failures); `forgejo-postgres` has the same failure mode.
Background: [ADR-002](docs/adr/002-multipart-corruption-detection-gaps.md),
[ADR-005](docs/adr/005-out-of-order-multipart-uniform-part-size.md),
[ADR-008](docs/adr/008-multipart-part-size-error-clarity.md).

ARMOR's side of this is done and correct: ADR-005's uniform-part-size
contract is enforced live, and ADR-008 shipped a clear, actionable rejection
message (`InvalidPartSize: Part size N is not a multiple of the block size
(65536 bytes)...`) instead of a silent failure. **This bead is not about
ARMOR's behavior being wrong — it is about characterizing why
barman-cloud-backup cannot satisfy ARMOR's documented, deliberate contract,
and deciding what (if anything) should change.**

## A same-day "fix" already failed — do not repeat this mistake

declarative-config commit `c8aefe75` (2026-08-06 08:50 EDT) disabled gzip
compression on both clusters' base-backup data
(`barmanObjectStore.data: {}`), on the theory that barman's tar streamer
flushes to S3 in exact 65536-byte chunks when uncompressed, so every part
boundary would land on a clean multiple of ARMOR's block size. The commit
message and manifest comments describe this as "verified empirically."

**That verification does not hold.** Live pod logs pulled *after* the fix
was deployed and synced (2026-08-06T21:03-21:04Z, many hours after the
08:50 EDT deploy) show both clusters still failing on every scheduled
attempt:

```
queue-db:          Part size 11876352 is not a multiple of the block size (65536 bytes)
forgejo-postgres:   Part size 4284416 is not a multiple of the block size (65536 bytes)
```

Overshoot analysis: `11876352 = 65536*181 + 14336` and `4284416 = 65536*65 +
24576`. Both remainders (14336, 24576) are exact multiples of 512 (POSIX
tar's block size) but NOT of 65536. This means barman-cloud-backup's real
flush granularity is NOT the 65536-byte unit the fix assumed — the "verified
empirically" claim was based on an insufficient one-off test, not on watching
real scheduled runs. (One `forgejo-postgres` run did succeed once, at 15:04Z
the same day — almost certainly because that particular backup's total size
happened to stay under barman's flush threshold and never triggered
multipart upload at all, not because the fix works.)

Two earlier CLI-flag-level workarounds were also tried on
`forgejo-postgres` and both failed live: `--min-chunk-size=5MB` and
`--min-chunk-size=2GB` (attempting to force a single-part upload). The 2GB
attempt still produced one misaligned part — expected, since ADR-005
deliberately does **not** exempt a lone first-and-only part from alignment
(only a genuinely trailing part *after* an already-aligned first part is
exempt — this is a poison-detection safeguard, not an oversight, added after
this project's real history of silent multipart corruption; see ADR-005 and
the historical incidents it links).

## What this bead is

1. **Actually characterize barman-cloud-backup 3.19.1's real
   upload/flush behavior** (the version confirmed live in both pods'
   tracebacks: `/usr/local/lib/python3.9/dist-packages/barman/cloud.py`).
   Do this locally, inside this checkout — no cluster access is needed or
   should be used:
   - Install `barman-cloud-backup` (pip, throwaway venv) and read
     `barman/cloud.py`'s `CloudTarUploader`/`CloudUploadController` upload
     path directly rather than re-guessing from outside behavior.
   - Reproduce the failure locally: run a local `cmd/armor` instance
     against a local/mock backend, drive a `barman-cloud-backup`-shaped
     (or literal) multipart upload of a realistic PostgreSQL-base-backup
     tar stream through it, and confirm you can reproduce non-65536-aligned
     part sizes with overshoot patterns matching the real evidence above
     (i.e. remainder is a clean multiple of 512, not 65536).
   - Determine precisely what would need to be true (client-side config,
     patch, or none-of-the-above) for barman-cloud-backup to reliably
     produce ARMOR-compliant part boundaries with data of arbitrary,
     unpredictable size.

2. **Write ADR-010** documenting the root cause and a recommendation.
   Plausible directions to weigh (not prescriptive — pick based on what the
   investigation actually finds):
   - A client-side-only fix exists and is real (not another "verified
     empirically" mistake) — document exactly what it is and why it's
     provably reliable across arbitrary data sizes, including the
     boundary cases ADR-005 cares about (short-first-part poisoning).
   - No reliable client-side fix exists with the current barman-cloud
     version, and ARMOR needs a deliberate, narrowly-scoped accommodation
     (e.g. an opt-in mode with a different integrity mechanism for clients
     that can't guarantee alignment). If recommending this, be explicit
     about how it avoids reintroducing the exact class of silent corruption
     ADR-002/003/005 already fought and fixed once.
   - These two backup targets should stop writing through ARMOR's direct
     S3 endpoint entirely for base backups (e.g. route through Garage the
     way `apexalgo-iad`/`ardenone-cluster` already do, with ARMOR/B2 as a
     secondary off-site copy instead of the primary barman target).

## Acceptance criteria

- Local reproduction that matches the real observed failure pattern
  (misaligned part with a 512-but-not-65536-byte-multiple remainder),
  not a hand-wavy "should be similar" — cite the actual numbers.
- ADR-010 written and added to `docs/adr/`, referencing ADR-002/003/005/008
  and this bead's evidence.
- Do **not** close this bead on the strength of one successful test run —
  today's incident is the second time in this exact saga that a single
  passing attempt was mistaken for a fix (see forgejo's 15:04Z run above,
  and the four prior "fixed, still corrupts" cycles documented in ARMOR's
  own git/bead history for this general class of bug). If proposing a fix,
  the acceptance test must be multiple consecutive successful runs against
  data sizes that vary (don't let a single lucky size hide non-determinism).
- Do not modify anything outside this repository. This bead needs no
  cluster or `declarative-config` access — deploying/verifying any resulting
  fix against the live `iad-ci` clusters is deliberately out of scope here
  (tracked separately, ops-gated).

issue.title: Root-cause barman-cloud-backup InvalidPartSize failures + write ADR-010

No kubeconfig grants secret-read or exec against commitgraph on ord-devimprint. All 3 static-token contexts (ord-devimprint-token, ord-devimprint-admin, ord-devimprint) return 401 Unauthorized; both OIDC contexts hang then time out (token cache empty, browser flow impossible headless). Observer is 403 by design. Other-cluster kubeconfigs are not candidates (commitgraph NotFound there). Auth-layer failure blocks both Path A (exec) and Path B (secret-read) identically.

Precise blocker report with per-operation matrix + root cause + exact Spot-dashboard OIDC refresh remediation appended to scratch/commitgraph-b2-access.md (Appendix A), committed 576f3a1b. issue.description:
THIS IS THE CORE BLOCKER. The two access paths both need RBAC beyond a read-only proxy: Path A needs pod-exec on queue-api; Path B needs secret-read on commitgraph-b2-workers. Read-only proxies grant NEITHER. Find which kubeconfig grants each. This is the gate the prior 3 failures never got past.

Context: bf-1q3s0v documents that admin OIDC kubeconfigs (e.g. ord-devimprint-admin) expire roughly every 3 days and time out when stale. Expect some to be dead; the goal is to find a LIVE one.

Tasks:
- Against the host cluster identified in the previous child, test each admin/direct kubeconfig in ~/.kube/ (e.g. ardenone-manager, rs-manager, apexalgo-iad, ord-devimprint-admin, iad-ci, iad-options) for TWO operations:
  (a) secret-read: `kubectl <kubeconfig> get secret commitgraph-b2-workers -n commitgraph -o jsonpath='{.data}'` succeeds;
  (b) exec: `kubectl <kubeconfig> exec <queue-api-pod> -c litestream -n commitgraph -- echo ok` succeeds.
- Record, per operation, the kubeconfig path that works (exec-capable and secret-read-capable may be different kubeconfigs).

## Acceptance Criteria
- EITHER a working kubeconfig path is recorded for exec AND/OR for secret-read against the commitgraph cluster; OR
- if NONE work, a precise blocker report is produced naming exactly which kubeconfig is stale/expired and what needs refreshing (mirror the bf-1q3s0v self-service Spot-dashboard OIDC refresh pattern). That blocker report is itself a closable, actionable outcome.
- Result appended to scratch/commitgraph-b2-access.md.
issue.notes:
[migrated notes from bf-3hvieu]
Probed every ord-devimprint direct/admin kubeconfig for BOTH operations (host cluster = ord-devimprint, per bf-3hbw6f). Re-confirmed live pod queue-api-c5894c469-pzjsl, litestream container.

RESULT: BLOCKED — no kubeconfig grants secret-read OR exec. Auth fails at the API layer, so it blocks both ops identically.

Per-context matrix (timeout-bounded; stale Spot OIDC hangs):
- ord-devimprint-token / token-context (ngpc-user): secret-read=401 Unauthorized, exec=401 Unauthorized — static token expired.
- ord-devimprint-admin / apexalgo-ord-devimprint (ngpc-user-apexalgo static): 401/401 — static token expired.
- ord-devimprint / apexalgo-ord-devimprint (ngpc-user static): 401/401 — static token expired.
- ord-devimprint-admin / apexalgo-ord-devimprint-oidc (oidc exec): TIMEOUT/TIMEOUT — OIDC cache empty (~/.kube/cache/oidc-login/org_KsELolwAOxl3Zxfm has only 0-byte .lock files, no token blob) + no browser headless.
- ord-devimprint / apexalgo-ord-devimprint-oidc (oidc exec): TIMEOUT/TIMEOUT — same.
- ord-devimprint-observer (devpod-observer SA): 403/403 — read-only by design (never grants these; known).

Other-cluster kubeconfigs (apexalgo-iad, ardenone-manager, rs-manager, iad-ci, iad-options, iad-kalshi incl. default ~/.kube/config) are NOT candidates: commitgraph namespace is NotFound on all of them (recon matrix §1). No cross-cluster RBAC.

Remediation (operator self-service, mirrors bf-1q3s0v): Rackspace Spot dashboard -> ord-devimprint -> regenerate admin kubeconfig (overwrites ~/.kube/ord-devimprint-admin.kubeconfig). Then prime the OIDC token cache ONCE from a browser-capable machine (run any kubectl against it, complete login.spot.rackspace.com SSO) so the exec path works headless. The freshly-downloaded kubeconfig also carries a static ngpc-user token usable headless immediately but it is short-lived (the Aug-07 20:01 regen's static token was already Unauthorized by Aug-09, <~37h) — temporary unlock only. A single refreshed ord-devimprint-admin kubeconfig grants BOTH secret-read and exec (same cluster-admin OIDC identity); no per-operation split needed.

issue.close_reason: Implemented fail-closed error for range-over-compressed objects. Added early compression check in handleShareRangeRequest that returns 416 (Range Not Satisfiable) with clear error message 'Range reads unsupported on compressed objects'. The fix prevents returning corrupt data from byte-range requests on compressed objects since zstd variable-length encoding destroys fixed-offset seeking. Verified that range requests still work correctly for uncompressed objects. All tests pass (go test ./internal/...).
issue.description:
Add explicit error return for byte-range requests over compressed objects. Compression destroys fixed-offset seeking (zstd is variable-length), so range-over-compressed must fail closed with clear error (416/400) rather than returning corrupt data.

Acceptance:
- Range request over compressed object returns 416/400 with clear error message
- Error message explains limitation ("range reads unsupported on compressed objects")
- Range requests over uncompressed objects still work
- go test ./internal/... passes
issue.title: Implement fail-closed error for range-over-compressed

issue.description:
## Context

Placeholder/follow-on to the investigation bead (parent, blocks this one).
That bead's job is to root-cause why barman-cloud-backup can't produce
ARMOR-compliant (65536-byte-aligned) multipart part boundaries for
`queue-db`/`forgejo-postgres` base backups on `iad-ci`, and write ADR-010
recommending a direction.

## What this bead is

**Do not start this until the parent bead's ADR-010 is written and its
recommendation is "ARMOR needs a code-side accommodation."** If ADR-010
concludes the fix is purely client-side (barman config/patch) or
architectural (route via Garage instead of ARMOR directly), this bead
should be closed as not-applicable with a note pointing at what actually
shipped instead — do not implement speculative code ahead of the decision.

If and when ADR-010 does call for an ARMOR-side change: implement exactly
what it specifies, as narrowly scoped as the ADR describes. Given this
project's repeated history of relaxed-alignment changes causing real silent
multipart corruption (ADR-002/003/005), any accommodation must:

- Be opt-in / explicitly scoped to the affected client(s), not a global
  relaxation of ADR-005's contract.
- Preserve (or explicitly replace with something equally strong) the
  integrity guarantee that a misaligned part currently gives up by being
  rejected outright.
- Ship with a real test that exercises `internal/crypto` through the actual
  handler path at a realistic scale — not a mock-backend test, and not a
  test capped at a toy size. This project's bead history (bf-28rb and others)
  has repeatedly had "passing" multipart tests that didn't touch the real
  failure mode; don't repeat that here.

## Acceptance criteria

- Only proceed if ADR-010 calls for this.
- New/changed behavior is covered by a real-crypto-path test at production
  scale, `go test -race ./...` green.
- ADR-010 updated (or a short follow-up ADR added) documenting what
  actually shipped and why, so the next person reading ADR-010 doesn't have
  to reverse-engineer the final implementation from the diff.
- No cluster/`declarative-config` access needed or used here — deploying the
  fix to `iad-ci` and verifying it against live scheduled backups is a
  separate, ops-gated bead.

That file was ARMOR's only test suite exercising a REAL B2 bucket + real Cloudflare CDN end-to-end: PutObject/GetObject roundtrip, range reads, HeadObject size correction, ListObjectsV2, DeleteObject, CopyObject, multipart upload (3 parts/15MB), 20MB streaming, conditional requests, presigned URLs, health/canary endpoints, and direct-B2-download verifying ciphertext.

Confirmed still missing today: `git ls-tree -r HEAD --name-only | grep '^tests/integration'` returns nothing, and `ls tests/` shows no integration/ subdirectory. Nobody has noticed:
- docs/plan/plan.md's Project Structure section and Testing Strategy > Integration Tests section still document tests/integration/ as present, running "against real B2 bucket + Cloudflare CDN".
- README.md links to tests/integration/README.md under Documentation -- dead link.
- bf-28rb ("Strengthen multipart integration test to verify actual content ... Confirm this test actually gates the image-build/CI pipeline") was closed "Completed" AFTER the directory was deleted, for work against a file that no longer existed.
- bf-180ohh ("Verify multipart integration test gates CI pipeline") was also closed "Completed" for the same non-existent suite.
- plan.md Phase 5 still cites bf-28rb's mock-backend caveat as the open concern, unaware the underlying file is gone entirely, not just mock-backed.

This is a real coverage regression, not Pluck noise: there is currently ZERO test in the repo that exercises ARMOR against a real B2 bucket + real Cloudflare CDN end-to-end. The other *_integration_test.go files still present in the repo (under internal/backend and internal/server -- covering multipart, auth, and credential scenarios) all use in-process mock backends, not real B2/Cloudflare.

issue.description: bf-59unr3 and bf-4qq1 instructed that all ARMOR multipart writers (including commitgraph clone workers and litestream) be pinned to sequential, block-aligned, no-retry part behavior. ADR-005's uniform-part-size contract made that obsolete: out-of-order and concurrent parts are now supported, and retries are idempotent. Sweep docs/plan/plan.md, docs/adr/, README, and consumer-facing notes for that guidance and retract it, replacing with the actual ADR-005 client contract (uniform part size P pinned from part 1; only the final part may be short; non-aligned intermediate parts get 400). Leaving it in place discourages clients from using parallel uploads that now work.

issue.description:
## Why
ord-devimprint hit Backblaze B2's Class C (metadata) transaction cap.
Direct AWS CLI to B2 from inside the cluster confirmed:
  AccessDenied (ListObjectsV2): Transaction cap exceeded.

The biggest single source of Class C calls is ARMOR's own `/readyz`
handler (internal/server/server.go:243), which on every readiness probe
runs:
    s.backend.List(ctx, s.config.Bucket, "", "", "", 1)
With Kubernetes readinessProbe period=10s and N replicas, that is
6×N List calls per minute against B2 — roughly 17,000/day for 2
replicas. B2's free Class C cap is 2,500/day; everything beyond that
returns 403 AccessDenied, which our clients log as a credentials
failure and our own readiness probe interprets as "backend down",
producing a self-reinforcing degraded state.

## Goal
Make the readiness probe correct without spending a B2 metadata
transaction per probe. Sub-tickets cover the implementation, tests,
and the deployment-side probe-period bump.
issue.title: Reduce B2 Class C transaction churn from /readyz canary

- Base64 decoding succeeds without errors
- Decoded output is written to /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt

### Commands
```bash
# Decode the value
base64 -d /tmp/litestream_key_id.b64 > /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt 2>&1

# Check exit code
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Decoding successful"
else

    cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt  # This contains error output
    exit 1
fi

# Verify output file is non-empty
if [ -s /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt ]; then
    echo "Decoded file is non-empty"
    ls -lh /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
else
    echo "ERROR: Decoded output is empty"
    exit 1
fi
```

Success: Decoding succeeds, output file exists and is non-empty.

Failure: Decoding fails or produces empty output — base64 file may be corrupted or not valid base64.

[migrated notes from bf-55xfah]
## Test-structure exploration — synthesis (part 4/4, feeds bf-3exlq8)

### Test infrastructure already in place
Decompression tests run against a filesystem-backed storage fake (backend.NewFSBackend on a temp dir) injected into a real Server via the NewWithBackend factory, so no live B2/Cloudflare is needed. Helpers in internal/server/share_decompress_test.go do the full lift: setupTestEnvironment/loadTestConfig wire env-driven config; encryptTestData generates DEK/IV, encrypts, and returns an ARMORMetadata with the Compressed flag controllable; storeTestObject assembles the on-disk envelope (header + ciphertext + HMAC table) and Put's it; compressData zstd-compresses a []byte; generateRandomData makes payloads; generateTestToken mints a presign share token. At the pure-library layer, internal/crypto/crypto_decompress_test.go has its own compressData and drives crypto.Decompress / crypto.IsCompressed directly. A test can go raw bytes -> compress -> encrypt -> store -> token -> GET in a few lines.

### Scenarios already covered
- crypto.Decompress (unit): happy-path zstd roundtrip; uncompressed passthrough; empty; sub-magic-length short data; roundtrips small/medium/large up to 1MB; error cases (corrupted payload after magic, truncated stream, magic-only bytes, partial frame).
- crypto.IsCompressed: magic present/absent, empty, too-short, partial-magic.
- Share endpoint = server.handleShare -> handleShareFullObject, the BUFFERED path (collects all decrypted blocks then crypto.Decompress(allDecrypted) at server.go:1175): compressed object decompresses to original; uncompressed served as-is; table-driven mix (uncompressed text/binary, compressed repeating/binary, legacy-no-flag); explicit legacy object; full compress->encrypt->store->GET->decompress roundtrip at 3 sizes; first-block zstd-magic detection.
- Share range request: ONE test (TestShareGET_RangeRequestWithCompression) that checks only the HTTP status (206/200), NOT the returned bytes.

### Likely missing test case (handoff to bf-3exlq8)
No test exercises the STREAMING decompression path in handlers.handleFullObjectStream (internal/server/handlers/handlers.go:963-975) — the main authenticated S3 GetObject route that wraps an io.Pipe decryptor in zstd.NewReader and io.Copy's decompressed bytes to the client, sets X-Armor-Decompressed: true (line 846), and omits Content-Length for compressed objects (lines 837-839). Every existing compressed-decompression test routes through the SHARE endpoint's separate BUFFERED path (server.handleShareFullObject -> crypto.Decompress(allDecrypted)), so the streaming zstd-on-a-pipe code, its headers, and its chunked-transfer behavior are entirely untested. (Secondary smaller gap: the share range path, handleShareRangeRequest server.go:1196, only calls IsCompressed for logging and never decompresses — serving raw compressed bytes — and its single test asserts only status, not content.)

issue.description:
WHY: ARMOR exists because of a 2026-03-27 data-loss incident, and other infrastructure (an archive-to-B2 pipeline) is blocked on ARMOR being trustworthy as a backup target. The single most catastrophic failure mode — losing the MEK — has no documented mitigation. docs/ has cloudflare-setup.md and dashboard.md but no DR/operations doc. The admin API already provides the needed primitives (README.md 'Admin API': /admin/key/verify, /admin/key/rotate, /admin/key/export?confirm=yes; canary at /armor/canary).

WORK: write docs/disaster-recovery.md covering:
1. MEK backup/escrow procedure: exporting via /admin/key/export, where escrow copies should live conceptually (offline/secret manager — describe properties, NOT actual locations or key values), and the rule that a MEK must never be rotated without first verifying escrow of the old MEK (per-file DEKs wrapped by a lost MEK are unrecoverable)
2. Restore drill: step-by-step recovery when the ARMOR deployment/config is lost but MEK + B2 bucket survive — fresh instance with same env config, /admin/key/verify against the canary, spot-check decrypt; reference the offline decrypt CLI (bead bf-16vq) as the server-less path
3. Key-rotation failure recovery: rotation is resumable via .armor/rotation-state.json (plan.md 'Key Rotation'); document how to detect a half-rotated bucket and resume, and the implication that bucket versioning is OFF so CopyObject overwrites in place
4. Multipart caveat: objects with sidecar HMAC tables at .armor/hmac/<sha256-of-key> — recovery must preserve the .armor/ tree, never 'clean it up'
5. What is NOT recoverable: data written after last backup, objects whose wrapped DEK metadata was destroyed

ACCEPTANCE:
- docs/disaster-recovery.md exists and is linked from README.md Documentation section
- Every step names the exact endpoint/env var/file it uses; no placeholder hand-waving
- Contains no real key material, bucket names, tokens, or hostnames — generic examples only
- A restore drill was walked through at least on paper against the current code (endpoints verified to exist in internal/server)
issue.title: Disaster-recovery runbook: MEK backup/escrow, restore drill, rotation-failure recovery

## Test Failure Analysis

### Failing Test
test_detect_invalid_colon_at_start

### Test Case
Input YAML: :value

Expected: Invalid (should detect colon at start without preceding key)
Actual: Valid (no error detected)

### Root Cause
The SyntaxValidator::validate_structure() method does NOT check for lines that start with a colon (:) without a preceding key.

Current validation only checks for document markers, block scalar indicators, anchor/alias definitions, and colon followed by value.

The missing check is for a colon appearing at position 0 (or first non-whitespace) without any key before it, which is invalid YAML syntax.

### Required Fix
Add validation in validate_structure() to detect and report an error when a line starts with a colon (after trimming whitespace).

Implement comparison and flagging logic for version drift.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Takes deployed tags (from child 1) and latest releases (from child 2) as input
- For each deployment, calculates:
  - Number of releases behind (count of releases between deployed tag and latest)
  - Days behind (difference in publish dates)
  - Whether any missed releases are correctness-labeled
- Flags deployments exceeding thresholds:
  - More than N releases behind (configurable, default 3)
  - More than M days behind (configurable, default 30)
  - ANY correctness-labeled release behind (always flag regardless of N/M)
- Outputs structured report with cluster, deployed_tag, latest_tag, releases_behind, days_behind, missed_correctness_releases
- Semantic version comparison handles v-prefixed and non-prefixed tags

This implements the core drift detection algorithm.
issue.title: Build drift detection logic

[migrated comment from bf-33lalg, 2026-08-09T16:40:15.194968846Z, author cli]
Test-function documentation for internal/server/share_decompress_test.go (7 test functions, lines 24–584).

ALL 7 TEST FUNCTIONS (one-line purpose each):

1. TestShareGET_CompressedObject (L24) — single-case — Stores a zstd-compressed object (compressed BEFORE encryption, Compressed=true), then GETs /share/<token> and asserts the response body byte-equals the ORIGINAL pre-compression data (i.e. the server decompressed correctly). Also asserts compressed bytes != original to prove compression actually occurred.

2. TestShareGET_UncompressedObject (L117) — single-case — Stores an uncompressed object (Compressed=false) and asserts GET returns the body byte-equal to the original, confirming no decompression path runs on uncompressed data.

3. TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior (L179) — TABLE-DRIVEN, 5 cases — Verifies decompression behavior across every object type, each carrying an explicit wantDecompression flag. Cases: uncompressed_small_text, uncompressed_binary_data (50KB), compressed_repeating_text, compressed_binary_data (100KB), legacy_object_no_compression_flag. Core assertions per case: (a) retrieved body byte-equals original pre-compression data; (b) when wantDecompression=true the output differs from the encryption input (decompression ran), when false it equals the encryption input (decompression bypassed); (c) armorMeta.Compressed == tc.compressed.

4. TestShareGET_LegacyObject (L321) — single-case — Stores an object with Compressed explicitly forced false (simulates pre-compression-metadata legacy objects) and asserts GET returns the body byte-equal to the original — legacy objects served unchanged, decompression path not triggered.

5. TestShareGET_RoundTrip (L383) — TABLE-DRIVEN, 3 cases — Exercises the full pipeline compress -> encrypt -> store -> GET -> decompress for varied sizes/types: small_text, medium_binary (100KB), large_binary (512KB). Core assertion: retrieved data byte-equals original (full round-trip integrity). Also LOGs (not fails) if compression did not reduce size.

6. TestShareGET_CompressionDetectionFromFirstBlock (L474) — single-case — Verifies compression is detectable from the first decrypted block via zstd magic bytes (crypto.IsCompressed true) on the compressed payload before storing, then asserts GET returns 200 with decompressed data byte-equaling the original.

7. TestShareGET_RangeRequestWithCompression (L537) — single-case — Stores a 200KB compressed object, issues GET with Range: bytes=0-9999, and asserts the response status is 206 (Partial Content) or 200 — i.e. range requests do not break on compressed objects.

TABLE-DRIVEN vs SINGLE-CASE:
- Table-driven (2): TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior (5 cases), TestShareGET_RoundTrip (3 cases).
- Single-case (5): TestShareGET_CompressedObject, TestShareGET_UncompressedObject, TestShareGET_LegacyObject, TestShareGET_CompressionDetectionFromFirstBlock, TestShareGET_RangeRequestWithCompression.

SHARED STRUCTURE: All tests build an in-memory filesystem backend, a Server via NewWithBackend, attach a presigner, then encrypt+store via the shared helpers (encryptTestData, storeTestObject, generateTestToken, compressData, generateRandomData). The table-driven tests are the broader-coverage ones; the single-case tests each isolate one specific behavior (compressed round-trip, uncompressed passthrough, legacy-compat, magic-byte detection, range requests).

This satisfies parent acceptance: "Current test structure documented".

issue.description:
## Child Bead: Validate decoded value is AWS access key format

This bead validates the decoded value matches AWS access key pattern.

### Prerequisites
- Previous child bead complete (bf-3c5vm: base64 decoded to plain text)

### Acceptance Criteria
- Decoded value starts with AKIA (standard AWS access key prefix)
- Value is exactly 20 characters long (standard AWS access key length)
- Value contains only alphanumeric characters (A-Z, 0-9)
- No whitespace, corruption, or binary data

### Commands
```bash
# Display the decoded value
echo "Decoded value:"
cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
echo ""

# Get the value (strip any whitespace)
VALUE=$(cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | tr -d '[:space:]')

# Check length
echo "Value length: ${#VALUE}"

# Validate AWS access key format (AKIA + 16 alphanumeric chars)
if echo "$VALUE" | grep -qE '^AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}$'; then
    echo "SUCCESS: Valid AWS access key format detected"
    echo "Value matches pattern: AKIA + 16 alphanumeric characters"
else
    echo "ERROR: Value does not match AWS access key format"
    echo "Expected: AKIA followed by 16 alphanumeric characters (total 20 chars)"
    echo "Got: $VALUE"
    exit 1
fi

# Verify no binary/corrupted data
if file /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | grep -q "text"; then
    echo "File is text data (not binary)"
else
    echo "WARNING: File may contain binary data"
    file /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
fi
```

Success: Decoded value matches AWS access key format (AKIA + 16 chars).

Failure: Value does not match expected format — may be wrong secret, corrupted, or not an AWS key.
issue.title: Validate decoded value is AWS access key format

issue.description: ARMOR encrypts every PUT (internal/crypto/encryptor.go) but never compresses. Parquet is already compressed so this is a no-op there, but litestream WAL/SQLite snapshots, tar.gz DR fixtures, and JSON manifests/provenance objects stored under .armor/ (internal/manifest, internal/provenance) would shrink meaningfully with zstd applied before encryption (compressing after encryption is useless — ciphertext doesn't compress). Add an opt-in ARMOR_COMPRESS env var (default off, matches ADR-006's opt-in pattern) that zstd-compresses the plaintext stream before it hits internal/crypto/encryptor.go, and records a compressed flag in the envelope/metadata (see crypto/envelope.go version-byte dispatch pattern) so GetObject knows to decompress after decrypt. Ties into the Cost Model table in README.md — real storage cost reduction for compressible payloads.
issue.title: Optional pre-encryption compression (zstd) for non-columnar objects

The only gate today is that confirm parameter. Still the highest-severity live gap, since the entire ARMOR security model rests on MEK secrecy and armor-apexalgo is a live ACB bucket.

The declarative-config manifests currently carry placeholder values. issue.close_reason: Loosened SigV4 region validation to accept any non-empty region in the Credential scope. buildStringToSign and getSigningKeyForCredential now take an explicit region parameter from the client's credential scope instead of using configured B2 region. Clients with region=auto, us-east-1, etc. now succeed with valid credentials; wrong secrets still rejected. Tests added.
issue.description:
## Problem

ARMOR validates incoming SigV4 signatures against its configured B2 region (e.g. `us-west-002`). Clients that sign with a different region in their Credential scope fail with:

```
AccessDenied: Invalid credentials
```

even though their access key / secret pair is correct. This has already bitten at least one caller on `ord-devimprint`: the devimprint workers hardcode `region_name='auto'` in their boto3 client (an R2 convention), which silently overrides `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`. Every PutObject against ARMOR was rejected on signature mismatch despite valid credentials.

The region check adds no real security or tenant-separation — ARMOR is a single-tenant proxy in front of a single B2 bucket. Region in the Credential scope is informational only; rejecting mismatches just turns ARMOR into a footgun for S3 clients written for R2, MinIO, or any non-AWS endpoint that historically ignores region.

## Fix

Accept any non-empty region string in the SigV4 Credential scope. The signature recomputation must still use whatever region the client claimed — otherwise the HMAC chain breaks — but ARMOR should **not** require the claimed region to match its own `ARMOR_B2_REGION` config.

Concretely in the verifier:

- Parse `Credential=<access_key>/<date>/<region>/s3/aws4_request`.
- Recompute the signing key using the parsed `<region>` (not the configured region).
- Compare the recomputed signature to the provided one.
- Accept if they match; reject only on real signature mismatch, missing/bad credential, or bad key ID.

## Acceptance

- Clients signing with `region='auto'`, `region='us-east-1'`, or `region='us-west-002'` all succeed when their access key / secret is valid.
- Clients with a wrong secret still get AccessDenied (signature mismatch).
- Clients with a bogus access key ID still get AccessDenied.
- Existing clients that correctly use `us-west-002` continue to work unchanged.
- Add a test covering at least `auto`, `us-east-1`, and the configured region, each with a valid and an invalid secret.

## Why this over fixing clients

There's a parallel option of patching each caller (devimprint worker code, any future caller) to read region from env or hardcode the right value. That's a losing game — every new S3 library or tool that's R2- or MinIO-flavored will repeat this trap, and each failure surfaces as "Invalid credentials" which points investigators at secrets, not region config. Making ARMOR tolerant once fixes it forever.
issue.title: Loosen SigV4 region validation — accept any region

issue.close_reason: Already implemented in commit ce8fd9c. The readyz endpoint now uses a canary-first strategy: when the canary monitor is running, IsHealthy() is the sole signal (zero backend calls). When canary is disabled, a cached HeadBucket probe (ARMOR_READYZ_CACHE_TTL, default 30s) serves as fallback. All acceptance criteria verified.
issue.description:
## Current behaviour
internal/server/server.go:242  func (s *Server) readyz
1. Checks `s.canary.IsHealthy()` — already cheap, in-memory.
2. Then unconditionally runs `s.backend.List(ctx, bucket, "", "", "", 1)`
   to verify backend connectivity. This is a Class C call every probe.

## Proposed behaviour
- Keep the canary in-memory check (it already validates round-trip via
  the canary monitor goroutine, which writes/reads on its own schedule).
- Replace the per-probe `List` with one of:
  a) Trust the canary alone — return 200 if `s.canary.IsHealthy()`,
     503 otherwise. Canary-monitor cadence becomes the source of truth.
  b) HEAD a single sentinel object (e.g. `_armor/healthcheck`) and
     cache the result in-memory for `ARMOR_READYZ_CACHE_TTL` seconds
     (default 30s). Misses cost 1 Class C call; hits cost zero.

Option (a) is simplest and matches what the canary already provides.
Option (b) is a fallback if we want a probe that also re-verifies the
backend faster than the canary's interval.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `/readyz` no longer issues a `List` against the backend on every
      request.
- [ ] When the canary monitor reports unhealthy, `/readyz` returns 503
      with a clear message naming which check failed.
- [ ] Canary-disabled mode (no monitor) still works — fall back to a
      cached single-object HEAD or an in-memory "last successful
      backend op" timestamp.
- [ ] Configuration option(s) added to README's env-var table.
issue.title: Replace /readyz List(bucket) with cheap HEAD-on-sentinel + canary status

issue.description:
When ARMOR proxies a B2 error whose message contains XML-special characters (e.g., '&' in 'Caps & Alerts page'), the writeError helper embeds the raw string directly into the <Message> element without escaping it. The resulting XML is malformed, causing clients that parse the error body (e.g., litestream's AWS SDK) to fail with a secondary XML parse error instead of a clean error code.

Repro: trigger a B2 TransactionCapExceeded — ARMOR returns:
  <Message>...Transaction cap exceeded, see the Caps & Alerts page...</Message>
but the & is unescaped, breaking clients.

Fix: use xml.EscapeText (or encode via xml.Marshal) when constructing the Message field in writeError / writeErrorXML.
issue.title: XML error responses don't escape special characters in the message field

This format matches AWS S3's standard response format and ensures compatibility with DuckDB httpfs timestamp parsing. HTTP headers continue to use http.TimeFormat as required by RFC 7232.
issue.description:
## Goal
Change ARMOR's S3 response date formatting so DuckDB httpfs can parse timestamps correctly.

## Approach
Based on investigation findings, update the identified code paths to use RFC3339/ISO 8601 format consistently. The HTTP `Last-Modified` header must remain in HTTP-date format per RFC 7232 — but the XML body LastModified fields and any other timestamp fields that DuckDB parses must use ISO 8601.

If the issue is in the XML body, verify the exact ISO 8601 format DuckDB expects (e.g., `2006-01-02T15:04:05.000Z` vs `2006-01-02T15:04:05Z`).

If the issue is that DuckDB parses HTTP headers, consider adding an ISO 8601 date header alongside the standard HTTP-date one, or ensure the XML body is the sole source DuckDB uses.

## Key Files
- `/home/coding/ARMOR/internal/server/handlers/handlers.go`
- Potentially `/home/coding/ARMOR/internal/backend/b2.go`

## Acceptance
- All S3 API responses use parseable ISO 8601 dates where DuckDB expects them
- Existing clients (boto3, s3cmd, rclone) still work (they accept both formats)
- No regression in encryption/decryption or other ARMOR functionality
issue.title: Fix date formatting in ARMOR S3 handlers for DuckDB compatibility

issue.description: Plan Phase 6 goal (docs/plan/plan.md, ADR-004) is to prove backups are CONTINUOUSLY restorable across the whole bucket. internal/restoreverifier/verifier.go getHistoricalSample() (around line 873-908) lists up to 1000 objects via a single unsorted backend.List() call, then does NOT randomly sample them despite the function name and the comment on it: it just slices candidates[len(candidates)-sampleCount:] (last N of whatever order List() returned), with an explicit TODO at line ~904: "Simple random sample (in production, use proper random sampling)" / "For now, just take the last N objects". Practical effect: verification systematically favors whatever objects land at the tail of one List page and can permanently starve older or differently-prefixed objects of ever being restore-verified, undermining the whole restorability guarantee Phase 6 exists to provide. Fix: implement real random sampling (e.g. reservoir sampling or crypto/math-rand shuffle+slice) across the full candidate set, and if the bucket has more than one List page worth of objects, paginate through ListObjects (using continuationToken) rather than sampling from only the first 1000-object page. Add/extend a unit test in internal/restoreverifier (using the existing mock backend pattern already used elsewhere in that package) asserting that repeated calls with a large synthetic candidate set produce different, roughly-uniform samples rather than always the same tail slice. No credentials or live cluster access needed — this is pure Go logic exercised via the mock backend, same as internal/restoreverifier/verifier_test.go.
issue.title: restore-verifier historical sampling picks last-N objects, not a random sample

issue.description:
## Why this is blocked, not open

This bead requires `kubectl` write access to `iad-ci` and push access to the
`jedarden/declarative-config` repo (a different repo from this checkout) to
actually deploy and verify anything. It is **not reachable from an
ARMOR-repo-scoped worker** and must not be picked up by one — set to
`blocked` deliberately, matching this project's established convention for
ops/credential-gated work (see e.g. the historical fencing of bf-4qq1,
bf-2t1f, bf-32ms, bf-5aqh0). A human, or an agent session with the relevant
kubeconfig and declarative-config write access, needs to pick this up
directly — not via `bf ready` dispatch.

## Background — read ADR-011, not ADR-010

ADR-010 (2026-08-06) originally recommended rerouting these backups to
Garage; that was reversed by explicit operator direction. **ADR-011**
(`docs/adr/011-barman-stays-on-armor-non-uniform-multipart.md`,
2026-08-07, supersedes ADR-010) is the current design: ARMOR's alignment
check was over-broad — part 1 and the presumed-final part never actually
needed block alignment (part 1 always starts at block 0; nothing follows
the final part). That exemption is **already shipped on main**
(`fc6c1a86`, `1f6e6934`) and, since both `queue-db` (~30MB) and
`forgejo-postgres` (~63MB) fit comfortably in a single multipart part
(S3's per-part ceiling is 5GiB), it resolves the outage **without** needing
non-uniform multipart support. That durable follow-on (for when these DBs
grow past one part) is tracked separately at `bf-57kgrx` and is **not** a
prerequisite for this bead.

## What needs to happen once unblocked

1. Deploy the current ARMOR main (containing `fc6c1a86`/`1f6e6934`) to
   `iad-ci`.
2. Configure both `k8s/iad-ci/queue-db/cnpg-cluster.yaml` and
   `k8s/iad-ci/forgejo/cnpg-cluster.yaml` in `declarative-config` with a
   barman `--min-chunk-size` large enough to force a single flush for each
   database's actual backup size (large enough that the whole backup fits
   before the first flush — the 2026-08-03/04 attempt at this failed only
   because the server-side part-1/final-part exemption didn't exist yet;
   it does now).
3. **Separately, fix the `ScheduledBackup` cron schedule on both
   clusters.** Both currently set `schedule: "0 4 * * *"` / `"0 3 * * *"`
   intending 5-field daily-at-4am/3am, but CNPG parses this as **6-field
   cron with seconds**, so it fires **hourly, at :04/:03 past every hour**
   (confirmed live 2026-08-06 and again 2026-08-07:
   `queue-db-daily-20260806140400`, `...150400`, `...160400`... one every
   hour). Per ADR-011: the fix is `0 0 4 * * *` / `0 0 3 * * *` (explicit
   leading `0` seconds field). Independently worth fixing regardless of
   the multipart issue — it's multiplying the failure/retry rate ~24x on
   single-instance CNPG clusters.
4. Verify by watching **real, live `Backup` objects** in both namespaces
   (`kubectl get backups -n queue-db`, `kubectl get backups -n forgejo`) —
   do not declare success from a manual/offline test or a single run.
   Given this saga's history (a same-day "verified empirically" fix on
   2026-08-06 turned out to still be failing hours later; ADR-011 itself
   notes its own fix is "committed but not yet confirmed in production"),
   require **multiple consecutive real `ScheduledBackup`-triggered runs**
   to complete successfully before treating this as fixed.
5. Add a short outcome addendum to ADR-011 (final deployed state, any
   deviation) — don't let this be the third unverified "fixed" claim in
   this saga's history.

## Acceptance criteria

- At least 2 consecutive real (not manual) `Backup` objects on each of
  `queue-db` and `forgejo-postgres` show `status: completed`.
- `ScheduledBackup` cadence confirmed to actually be daily, not hourly
  (`0 0 4 * * *` / `0 0 3 * * *` or equivalent, live-verified against
  actual `Backup` object creation timestamps over 24h+, not just the
  schedule string).
- ADR-011 updated with the final, verified outcome.

issue.description:
Context: InitB2Backend in internal/backend/secondary_init.go has a doc comment (lines 99-104) that already CLAIMS it runs an explicit HeadBucket connectivity probe, but the implementation at line 153 returns NewB2Backend(ctx, b2Cfg) directly with no probe. NewB2Backend (internal/backend/b2.go:44) is lazy — it loads static credentials and constructs the S3 client but makes NO network call — so InitB2Backend currently succeeds offline for any syntactically valid config regardless of whether the endpoint is reachable or the credentials authenticate. This child adds the probe the doc comment already promises. Depends on sibling "Wire HeadBucket probe..." being done first... actually this IS that first step.

Acceptance Criteria:
- In InitB2Backend (internal/backend/secondary_init.go:128), capture the typed *B2Backend returned by NewB2Backend into a local instead of returning it directly at line 153.
- After successful construction, run a connectivity probe: call b2.HeadBucket(ctx, cfg.Bucket) (already exists at internal/backend/b2.go:526). This is the call where credential rejection and endpoint-unreachable failures actually surface (the AWS SDK defers auth to the first request).
- On probe failure return (nil, err) where err wraps the probe cause with high-level context, e.g. fmt.Errorf("b2 backend initialization failed: %w", err). Do NOT return the partially-constructed backend on probe failure.
- On probe success, return the constructed backend.
- NewB2Backend's own construction error (b2.go:54 "failed to load AWS config") must still propagate; wrap it the same way for consistency.
- Do NOT change validateB2Config or the defensive type-check guard.

Scope: implementation + error wrapping + nil-backend guarantee ONLY. Tests are the next two children.

Verified empirically: a fake-cred config now surfaces 'b2 backend initialization failed: HeadBucket failed: ... api error Forbidden: Forbidden'. go build + go vet clean.

IMPORTANT FOR SIBLING TEST BEADS: the committed internal/backend/secondary_init_test.go::TestInitB2BackendFromConfig has TWO offline-success sub-cases ('valid config returns initialized B2 backend' and 'empty type allowed with valid B2 fields') that relied on NewB2Backend being lazy (fake creds KEYID/SECRET vs real endpoint s3.us-east-005.backblazeb2.com, wantErr:false). These now FAIL because HeadBucket makes a real network call and gets 403 Forbidden. The 6 validation/type-check sub-cases still pass. The success sub-cases need rewriting to point HeadBucket at a local mock S3 server (httptest) returning 200, plus a new probe-failure sub-case (403 -> nil backend, error containing 'b2 backend initialization failed'). ## Acceptance Criteria

1. Check out the clean git version: `git show HEAD:internal/server/server.go > /tmp/git-server.go`
2. Run line-by-line diff: `diff -u /tmp/git-server.go /tmp/running-server.go > /tmp/server-go-diff.txt`
3. Check exit code: 0 = MATCHES, 1 = DRIFTS
4. Output status to stdout: "server.go: MATCHES" or "server.go: DRIFTS"

## Notes

issue.description:
Feature-completeness gap and the most design-sensitive piece. The multipart PUT path (internal/server/handlers/handlers.go ~L2550 NewEncryptor + EncryptWithStartingCounter) never calls crypto.Compress or header.SetCompressed. Multipart uploads bypass compression entirely, so large multi-part objects get no storage savings; and if a multipart object were ever marked compressed, CTR part-offset math (ADR-005: part N starts at block (N-1)*P/BlockSize) would break because zstd framing is variable-length, not block-aligned.

Depends on child 1's round-trip harness and child 2's reader fixes; extend the harness to multipart.

Decide and implement the composition of compression with multipart. Two viable designs:
(a) Compress each part independently before EncryptWithStartingCounter and record per-part compressed sizes so the CTR block-alignment invariant holds on the COMPRESSED byte stream (part N startBlockIndex from cumulative compressed bytes — requires recording each part's compressed length in upload state); OR
(b) Fail closed at CreateMultipartUpload when ARMOR_COMPRESS=true (reject/disable compression on the multipart path), documenting that multipart objects are stored uncompressed while single-PUT objects still benefit.

Pick (a) ONLY if it preserves ADR-005's idempotent-retry byte-identical-ciphertext property; otherwise pick (b) as the safe default. Record the decision + tradeoff for child 4 (ADR-007).

Acceptance:
- Multipart upload under the chosen design round-trips byte-identical via multipart GET.
- ADR-005 out-of-order / idempotent-retry invariants preserved (existing internal/crypto/multipart_*_test.go tests still pass).
- Decision captured for child 4 to document.
- go test ./internal/... passes.
issue.title: Wire zstd compression into the multipart upload path

issue.description:
ARMOR's canary and integration tests never exercise the real, client-facing S3 HTTP API end-to-end -- and never test the full object lifecycle (write through delete). This is a genuine coverage gap distinct from the multipart/HMAC bug: the code path a real client (aws-cli, litestream, kalshi-tape's writer) actually hits is `internal/server/handlers` over HTTP; the canary (`internal/canary/canary.go` check()/checkMultipart()) calls `m.backend.Put`/`CreateMultipartUpload`/`UploadPart`/`CompleteMultipartUpload`/`GetRangeWithHeaders`/`Delete` DIRECTLY against the backend package, bypassing the HTTP handler layer, routing, auth/ACL enforcement, and the exact sidecar-detection logic that caused bf-24sxh7 (GET path ignoring the multipart marker). A regression isolated to the HTTP layer -- like bf-24sxh7 itself -- would not be caught by the canary as it exists today; it took a hand-run litestream restore to find that bug.

Additionally, no test (canary or integration) exercises the FULL file lifecycle. Confirmed gaps as of 2026-07-22:
- DELETE is fire-and-forget in both canary checks (`go func() { ... m.backend.Delete(...) }()`, cleanup errors silently swallowed) -- there is no assertion that delete succeeds, and no test that a deleted key actually returns 404/NoSuchKey on a subsequent GET/HEAD, or disappears from LIST.
- No overwrite/update-in-place coverage: writing the same key twice (a real pattern for litestream and other continuous writers) is never verified.
- No LIST coverage at all: nothing asserts an uploaded object appears in ListObjects, or that a deleted one stops appearing.
- Multipart Abort is only exercised as an error-handler side effect on failure paths, never as its own deliberate test -- and nothing verifies Abort actually removes the incomplete upload on the B2 side. This is not hypothetical: a 2026-07-20 B2 hygiene pass found a real pile of ABANDONED incomplete multipart uploads left over from pre-fix concurrent-part failures, still accruing B2 storage cost.

## Acceptance criteria (write these BEFORE closing -- this repo has closed this exact bead 4 times on insufficient evidence, see bf-1v6skf)

1. A test (extended canary cycle or integration test) issues REAL HTTP requests against ARMOR's actual S3-compatible listener (SigV4-signed, via an S3 SDK or equivalent), not direct internal `backend.*`/`crypto.*` package calls. Must run against a real backend (B2), not `mockBackendForMultipart` -- per bf-28rb's exact prior lesson, a mock-backed test does not count as coverage of this bead.
2. Covers, in one continuous lifecycle per test run: PUT (single-part), PUT (multipart, >=2 parts, non-final part >=5MiB), HEAD, GET (full download, byte-exact), GET (byte-range, including a range that straddles both a part boundary and a block boundary), LIST (key appears with correct size), overwrite (PUT the same key again with different content, verify the new content wins on next GET), DELETE, and post-delete verification: GET returns 404/NoSuchKey, HEAD returns 404, LIST no longer includes the key.
3. Separately exercises multipart Abort as its own deliberate case (not just as an error-path side effect): create upload, upload >=1 part, Abort, then assert via ListMultipartUploads (or equivalent) that the incomplete upload is actually gone on the B2 side -- not just that the local call returned success.
4. Closure requires citing the actual HTTP status codes / response bodies from a live run (or a CI log for the gating integration test) as evidence -- a passing test function name or green CI badge alone is not sufficient, consistent with every other verification bar on this repo's Phase 5/6 work.

Related: bf-24sxh7 (the exact HTTP-layer-only bug this gap would have caught earlier), bf-1v6skf (canary bypass noted in comment 94 as a follow-up), bf-4595 (multipart canary extension -- this bead extends that work to the full lifecycle + HTTP layer rather than only upload/download).

issue.description: Read path assumes single-PUT layout: header, data, embedded HMAC table. Multipart-completed objects are raw concatenated part ciphertext with no header and the HMAC table in a sidecar; a multipart marker is set in object metadata on complete. No reader-side code checks that marker, so every GET of a multipart object 500s with prefetch offset out of range; the Range path shares the assumption. Repro: TestMultipartFullCycleByteVerification in the handlers test package (file multipart_routing_test.go), skip-gated on this bead. Fix both full-object and range paths. See the upload-retrieval test matrix doc, rows U4 R4 R7.

issue.close_reason: Fixed misleading WARN when B2 key is bucket-scoped. When ARMOR_BUCKET is set (production config), the B2 application key is scoped to a single bucket and cannot call account-level B2 API endpoints like b2_authorize_account. Previously, ARMOR would attempt to create the B2 keys client regardless, resulting in a 401 error logged as WARN. Now, when ARMOR_BUCKET is set, we skip the B2 keys client initialization entirely and log at INFO level. S3 read/write paths unaffected - S3 backend created independently using same credentials.
issue.description:
## Problem

At startup ARMOR logs:

```
WARN  Failed to create B2 keys client - key management disabled
      error: b2_authorize_account: 401:
```

...whenever the configured B2 application key is scoped to a single bucket (the production/recommended configuration). Bucket-scoped app keys authenticate correctly for S3 ops against their bucket but **cannot** call the account-level `b2_authorize_account` endpoint that the keys-management subsystem needs. The 401 is returned by B2 by design.

This has caused false-alarm investigations on both `ardenone-hub` (bucket `armor-apexalgo`) and `ord-devimprint` (bucket `devimprint`) — operators saw the WARN, assumed credentials were broken, and chased it before realizing S3 traffic was flowing fine.

## Fix

Detect the bucket-scoped case and either:

1. **Preferred**: if `ARMOR_BUCKET` is set, skip the keys-client init entirely and log at INFO: `B2 key management disabled (application key is bucket-scoped)`.
2. **Minimum**: downgrade the log level to INFO and rewrite the message so it reads as expected behavior, not a failure. E.g.: `B2 key management unavailable — application key lacks account-level scope (this is normal when ARMOR_BUCKET is set)`.

Option 1 avoids even making the failing API call; option 2 keeps current behavior but stops scaring operators.

## Acceptance

- Starting ARMOR with a bucket-scoped B2 key emits no WARN or ERROR about `b2_authorize_account`.
- S3 read/write paths still work identically.
- If someone misconfigures a truly invalid key (wrong id/secret), they still get a clear error at S3-op time.
issue.title: Suppress misleading WARN when B2 key is bucket-scoped
